tts_summary:
Here's your after-the-close recap for Thursday, September 24th. Four names to walk through — Akamai, Costco, Lear, and T-Mobile. Let's start with the biggest one.

Akamai is the headline tonight. The company announced a major expansion of its AI compute infrastructure relationship with Anthropic — an $11.6 billion contractual commitment over seven years, with the possibility of an additional $9 billion on top, bringing the total potential deal value to $20 billion. This cements Akamai's positioning as what the note calls an edge neocloud, leaning hard into AI infrastructure as an alternative to the hyperscalers. But the deal is not cheap. Capex associated with just the base $11.6 billion is estimated at roughly $5.5 billion — that's nearly half the committed revenue flowing right back out the door in capital spending. And Akamai is handing Anthropic warrants for up to 5% of shares outstanding at an exercise price of $111.33, with 2% vesting immediately. Lenovo and Jabil are expected to play meaningful roles supplying infrastructure for the buildout. The revenue guidance for 2026 is unchanged, but capex is set to spike. Net net — directionally exciting for the AI infrastructure theme, but the economics require scrutiny.

Costco reported fiscal fourth quarter results. Headline EPS came in at $6.75, but $0.15 of that was tariff refunds. Strip those out and you're at $6.60, which is a modest beat versus the Street's $6.53. Membership fee revenue — being disclosed for the first time this quarter since merchandise sales were already known — came in at $1.85 billion versus expectations of $1.832 billion, a slight positive. Renewal rates ticked up 10 basis points sequentially both globally and in the US and Canada. Headline comps were plus 9.4%, or plus 6.7% excluding gas and foreign exchange. Merchandise gross margins were essentially in line. The bottom line here is that this was a decent but not exciting print — membership trends are holding, but the headline beat was partly manufactured by refunds.

Lear expanded its buyback authorization from $600 million to $1.5 billion — that's roughly 26% of the current market cap. The board cited confidence in free cash flow generation. That's a strong signal from management and a meaningful return of capital commitment.

Finally, T-Mobile raised its dividend 15% to $1.17 per share, taking its yield to 2.83%. Sounds good on its own, but context matters — AT&T yields 4.36%, Verizon yields 5.98%, and the 10-year Treasury is sitting at 5.21%. T-Mobile's income appeal remains limited in this rate environment.

The overarching theme tonight is AI infrastructure spend continuing to flow, with Akamai as tonight's clearest expression of that trade — just watch the capex drag and the dilution.
